name: Yusuf Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I keep sheep on Carrow Fell, about six hundred ewes on rough hill grazing that runs up to the ridge, plus forty hectares of better fields down by the house. Most days start at half six with the quad bike and the dogs, checking the ewes, then fencing, or fixing the water troughs that freeze up there in winter. My wife Hana's father, Idris, farmed it for forty years, and when his hip went three years ago we sold our house in town and moved up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: So you came to it late. What did you do before?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nineteen years driving buses for the city, and I was a union rep at the depot for the last eight of those. I know timetables and drivers' rights, not sheep, and I'm still learning. Idris sits in the kitchen and tells me what I did wrong by looking at the ewes from the window, and he's usually right.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the quiet up top, and I like that when a lamb lives it's because somebody stayed up for it. Lambing wears me out, three weeks in April where I sleep in two-hour pieces in the shed. Our boy Zaid is twelve and he's better with the dogs than I am, which is a bit humbling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first of five pictures of the next five years. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, good luck to them. A search engine doesn't walk up the fell in sleet to find a ewe stuck on her back. It doesn't change anything up here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it means nothing for me. I've got a flip phone, and Hana does all the online forms for the farm payments. I didn't come up here to stare at a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as I'm doing now. Get the new fence up along the top boundary before tupping, which is when the rams go in with the ewes, and sell the lambs at the October sale in town. Maybe go on the sheep scanning course the co-op runs, if it's still running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. It's other people's weather, if you know what I mean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sold a house in town to come here. Is that money still sitting somewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of it, yes, about a year and a half of living money in the building society, and a bit in my bus pension. Hana and I agreed we don't touch it for the farm unless the roof goes. It's what lets me sleep, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about something like this, at the mart or in the village?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly Owen, who farms the next hill and sits next to me at the lamb sales. He'd say the same as me, that it's for office people. We'd talk about lamb prices for an hour and AI for about a minute.

S0.say: I'd tell people it doesn't change anything up on the hill. A better search engine won't walk up the fell in sleet to find a ewe stuck on her back.
S0.think: Privately I think it means nothing for me at all. I have a flip phone and Hana does the online farm forms, and I didn't come up the hill to stare at a screen.
S0.do: Carries on as now: finishes the top boundary fence before the rams go in and sells lambs at the October sale. Looks into the co-op's sheep scanning course and leaves the building society savings untouched.
S0.feel: Calm. He sees it as somebody else's weather.
S0.quote: A search engine doesn't walk up the fell in sleet to find a ewe stuck on her back.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf frames the whole subject as office business, far from the hill. His savings from the house sale are clearly a big part of his calm, and he says so himself. The bus depot years show in how he talks about rules and fairness, even here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's move to the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same old story with a new coat on. Firms always find a reason to hire fewer young people. At the depot it was cameras and computer timetables, and before that it was something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the bit about fewer beginners gets me. Up here the young ones already leave for town, and if the agricultural college and the vets' practice take on fewer trainees, there's nobody to learn from. I'm a beginner myself, really, at forty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign Zaid up for the young farmers' club and pay for him to do the shearing course next summer, so he's got a skill in his hands. And I'd keep pushing at the farmers' union meetings for the government to pay farms to take on trainees. That's about it, the sheep don't care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, not for me but for the next lot. It's slow, so you can see it coming and still not stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You called yourself a beginner. Who taught you, and who's teaching the next one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Davey, who shepherded for Idris for thirty years, taught me most of it before he retired last spring. He'd stand next to me at a difficult lambing and not say a word until I'd got it wrong twice. If firms stop paying for beginners, there won't be any more Daveys, because nobody pays you to be slow for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use one of these AI tools yourself, if it was slow and steady like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. Hana might, for the paperwork, and that's her business. I'd rather ring the vet and hear a person tell me I'm wrong.

S1.say: I'd say it's the same old story with a new coat on, because firms always find a reason to hire fewer young people. At the bus depot it was cameras and computer timetables.
S1.think: Privately, the part about fewer beginners worries me, because the young already leave the hill for town. I'm a beginner myself at forty-three, and I wonder who will train the next ones.
S1.do: Pays for his son Zaid to do a shearing course next summer and signs him up for the young farmers' club. Pushes at farmers' union meetings for public money to help farms take on trainees.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly for the next generation rather than himself. He feels he can see it coming and still can't stop it.
S1.quote: If firms stop paying for beginners, there won't be any more Daveys, because nobody pays you to be slow for two years.
S1.fieldNote: His worry here isn't his own job but the chain of teaching he depends on. Old Davey comes up with real warmth. The union rep is very close to the surface: his first move is a meeting and a demand for public support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the bosses doing what bosses do, cutting staff and calling it progress. I'd be on the side of the office workers, same as I was for the drivers. Politicians shouting doesn't help anybody, they want a proper plan for the people laid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the sheep are safe and I'm safe. But Hana's sister works in an insurance office, and my cousin Bilal is in a call centre, and they'd be the ones hurt. And when town people lose their wages, they buy less lamb, and the price at the sale goes down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a closer eye on the money and hold off on buying the second quad bike we talked about, which is about eight thousand. I'd go to the union branch and see if there's any campaign worth backing for the office lot. And I'd tell Bilal he can come up for lambing if he needs the work, though he'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm sorry for them and a bit relieved for me, and I don't like feeling relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd offer Bilal lambing work. What would that actually look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three weeks of nights in the shed, on a fair wage, which is more than Idris paid Davey at the start. Bilal has never touched a sheep, he'd faint at his first difficult birth. But it would be a wage and a roof, and that's what family is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about it, if they asked at tea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mariam, she's nine, that some grown-ups are losing their jobs to computers and it isn't their fault. And I'd tell Zaid the same thing I always tell him, learn something you can do with your hands. He rolls his eyes at that now.

S2.say: I'd say it's bosses cutting staff and calling it progress, and I'd stand with the office workers like I did for the bus drivers. I want a real plan for people laid off, not politicians shouting.
S2.think: Privately I think the sheep and my own work are safe, but my sister-in-law and my cousin in offices would be hurt. And when town people have less to spend, the lamb price at the sale goes down.
S2.do: Puts off buying a second quad bike, about eight thousand, and watches spending more closely. Goes to his union branch to look for a campaign to back, and offers his cousin Bilal paid lambing work.
S2.feel: Uneasy, with a mix of sympathy for others and a relief about his own work that he doesn't like in himself.
S2.quote: I'm sorry for them and a bit relieved for me, and I don't like feeling relieved.
S2.fieldNote: The relief and guilt sit right next to each other, and he names it himself without being asked. He links office layoffs straight to lamb prices, which is sharper economics than he gives himself credit for. Family is his safety net for other people, not just for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains belong to the people who did the work, not to whoever owns the computers. I'd back a proper tax on those companies and spend it on wages and training. I'd say that in the pub and I wouldn't care who heard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a house price boom is strange for us, because we already sold in town. Land prices up here might go up too, and then some rich person from the city wants a hill for the view and the sheep get pushed off. That's what I'd really be thinking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Hana and Idris and talk about whether we buy the forty hectares Owen rents next door before the city money does. We've got the savings for a deposit, just about. I'd also write to our member of parliament, in a letter, because I don't do email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's mostly anger at who gets rich, and under that a bit of worry for the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd use your savings to buy land. Earlier you said you don't touch that money unless the roof goes. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point, you've caught me. It's still the roof, in a way, because if the field next door goes to someone who plants trees for carbon money and shuts the gate, we lose our winter grazing. I'd need Hana to agree, and she'd make me sleep on it for a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you picture getting rich in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who already have shares, the ones on the business news in their nice jackets. Not Owen, not me, not the lad who drives the feed lorry. It would be like the bus company again, where the shareholders got a bonus the same year they cut the night routes.

S3.say: I'd say the gains belong to the people who did the work, not whoever owns the computers. I'd back a proper tax on those companies, spent on wages and training, and I'd say it in the pub.
S3.think: Privately I worry city money will push up hill land prices and buy farms for the view or for planting trees. Losing the grazing next door scares me more than anything to do with AI itself.
S3.do: Talks with Hana and Idris about using savings as a deposit on the forty hectares next door before outside buyers move in. Writes a paper letter to his member of parliament about taxing the gains.
S3.feel: Mostly angry about who gets rich, with an undercurrent of worry for the farm.
S3.quote: It would be like the bus company again, where the shareholders got a bonus the same year they cut the night routes.
S3.fieldNote: When challenged on the savings he laughed and admitted the contradiction, then reframed buying land as protecting the farm. His anger is clearly aimed at owners and shareholders, never at the technology itself. The bus company story seems to be his template for how change goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hill will be the last place a robot comes, and I'd believe it in public. Have you seen Carrow Fell in February? Machines get stuck in the bog by the lower gate, I've had a quad bike up to its seat in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me, but not because of my hill. The big lowland sheep farms with flat fields will get robots first, they'll produce lamb cheaper, and the price drops for everybody. I can't compete with a robot that doesn't sleep at lambing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every farmers' union meeting going and push for rules that the farm payments go to farms that keep people working, not to farms that buy machines. I'd ask Idris what he did in the eighties when prices crashed. And I'd tell Hana we keep the savings exactly where they are, no land, no nothing, until we see where it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, if I'm honest, and stubborn with it. I'm not leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you cut first if the lamb price fell by a third?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The contractor who does our silage, about three thousand a year, I'd do it myself with Idris's old mower even if it took me a week. Then the kids' riding lessons, which would break Mariam's heart. The mortgage on the shed loan stays paid, whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use AI tools. If a robot shepherd could do the night checks at lambing, would you buy one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Maybe I'm a fool, but no. Davey would come back and haunt me, and I'd deserve it.

S4.say: I'd say the hill will be the last place robots come, because machines get stuck in the bog on Carrow Fell. I've had a quad bike up to its seat in it.
S4.think: Privately I'm scared the flat lowland sheep farms will use robots to produce cheaper lamb and drag my price down. I can't compete with a machine that doesn't sleep at lambing.
S4.do: Pushes at farmers' union meetings for farm payments to reward farms that keep people employed. Keeps the savings untouched, drops plans to buy land, and would cut the three-thousand silage contractor first if prices fell.
S4.feel: Frightened and stubborn at the same time. He says plainly that he isn't leaving.
S4.quote: I can't compete with a robot that doesn't sleep at lambing.
S4.fieldNote: This is the first scenario where his calm public line and private view split sharply. He wouldn't buy a robot even if it helped him, and he knows it may be foolish. Price, not job loss, is the threat he sees, and his answer is collective: rules and union pressure.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, the robots, because it comes for the price of lamb, not for my job. What would help is farm payments that go to farms with people on them, and a fair floor price so the big flat farms can't undercut the hill. And I'd want the union to have a seat at the table when they write those rules.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Hana. She left a good job at the council office to come up here, and in the third picture her old job is the one that goes. Some nights I think we got out just in time, and some nights I think we ran away.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: What would you want people to understand about farmers like you?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: That being new at forty-three isn't a joke. I'm still learning every day, and I'd like the chance to finish learning before anybody decides this way of life is out of date.

headlineQuote: Some nights I think we got out just in time, and some nights I think we ran away.
portrait: Yusuf Ibrahim is a former city bus driver and union rep who moved his family onto his father-in-law's hill sheep farm three years ago and is still learning the work. Savings from selling their town house keep him calm through the first scenarios, which he treats as office business. His concern grows with the fewer-beginners and land-price pictures, and in the robot scenario he fears cheaper lowland lamb rather than losing his own job. He won't touch AI or robots himself, and his answer to every threat is collective: union meetings, letters and rules on who gets public money.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario worries him most, because robot-run lowland farms could drive down the price of lamb that his hill farm depends on.
whatWouldHelp: Farm payments that go to farms with people working on them, a fair floor price for lamb, and a seat for the farmers' union when the rules are written.
